Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Neural Functional Networks (NFNs)—models that process the weights of other neural networks as input data—have demonstrated significant potential in tasks such as implicit neural representation editing, learnable optimization, and generalization prediction. However, current NFN architectures are predominantly designed for Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Despite the dominance of Transformer architectures in modern deep learning (NLP, Vision, etc.), there is currently no systematic framework for applying NFNs to Transformers. Standard methods that flatten weights into vectors fail to respect the complex structural symmetries of the Transformer (e.g., the interchangeability of attention heads), leading to inefficient learning and poor generalization when processing these weight spaces.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that by mathematically characterizing the "maximal symmetric group" of the Transformer architecture—specifically within the Multi-Head Attention (MHA) mechanism and the Feed-Forward networks—we can construct an equivariant meta-architecture capable of processing Transformer weights effectively. We hypothesize that an NFN designed to be equivariant to these specific symmetries (such as head permutations and internal basis transformations) will be able to learn robust representations of Transformer models, treating functionally equivalent models as identical inputs.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We aim to develop "Transformer-NFN," a specialized architecture for processing the parameters of Transformer blocks. Our approach involves the following conceptual stages:

1.  **Symmetry Characterization:**
    We will formally derive the sufficient conditions under which two sets of Multi-Head Attention parameters define the same function. We anticipate that this symmetry group involves a combination of:
    *   **Head Permutations:** The independence of attention heads implies invariance to their reordering.
    *   **Linear Transformations:** Invertible linear mappings applied to the internal dimensions of Query, Key, and Value projections that cancel out in the final attention output.

2.  **Weight Space Construction:**
    We will define the input space not as a flat vector, but as a structured collection of weight tensors (Query, Key, Value, Output, and MLP weights). We will define a specific "group action" where the identified symmetries act upon this weight space.

3.  **Equivariant Polynomial Layers:**
    We propose to design the core layers of our NFN based on parameter-sharing principles.
    *   **Input Features:** Instead of operating solely on individual weight matrices, we will incorporate quadratic terms (specifically the products of Query-Key and Value-Output weights). This aligns the NFN's input with the actual functional mechanics of self-attention.
    *   **Equivariance constraint:** The layers will be constrained such that transforming the input Transformer weights (via the identified group action) results in an equivalent transformation of the NFN's features. This effectively hard-codes the "grammar" of the Transformer architecture into the processing network.

4.  **Invariant Pooling:**
    To generate final predictions (e.g., predicting the test accuracy of a given Transformer checkpoint), we will stack these equivariant layers followed by invariant layers. These final layers will aggregate features across the symmetric dimensions (like summing over heads), producing an output that is invariant to the symmetries of the input model.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Foundation:** We expect to provide the first rigorous mathematical characterization of the maximal symmetric group for Multi-Head Attention and standard Transformer blocks.
2.  **Novel Architecture:** The introduction of the Transformer-NFN, a meta-model capable of processing Transformer weights while respecting their functional symmetries.
3.  **Benchmarking Resource:** To facilitate this line of research, we intend to generate and release a large-scale "model zoo" dataset consisting of thousands of trained Transformer checkpoints across vision and text tasks, serving as a testbed for weight-space learning.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Small Transformer Zoo:** A dataset of over 125,000 Transformer model checkpoints trained on two tasks.
        *   **MNIST-Transformers:** 62,756 checkpoints of Vision Transformers trained on digit image classification (MNIST).
        *   **AGNews-Transformers:** 63,796 checkpoints of Transformers trained on text topic classification (AGNews).
    *   Checkpoints were generated by varying hyperparameters including train fraction, optimizer (SGD, SGDm, Adam, RMSprop), learning rate, L2 regularization, weight initialization standard deviation, and dropout.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Kendall’s $\tau$ rank correlation:** Measures the rank correlation between the predicted accuracy and the ground truth test accuracy of the input neural networks. Range is $[-1, 1]$.
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **MLP:** Multi-layer Perceptron taking flattened weights as input.
    *   **STATNN** (Unterthiner et al., 2020): Computes statistics of weights as input features.
    *   **XGBoost** (Chen & Guestrin, 2016): Gradient boosting on flattened weights.
    *   **LightGBM** (Ke et al., 2017): Gradient boosting on flattened weights.
    *   **Random Forest** (Breiman, 2001): Ensemble learning on flattened weights.
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Transformer-NFN Architecture:**
        *   Embedding component processed by a single-layer MLP (10 hidden neurons).
        *   Classifier component processed by a two-layer MLP (10 hidden neurons).
        *   Transformer block weights processed by an equivariant polynomial layer (10 hidden channels), followed by an invariant polynomial layer and an MLP.
        *   Outputs concatenated and passed to a final MLP head with Sigmoid activation.
    *   **Training Configuration:**
        *   Optimizer: Adam.
        *   Maximum Learning Rate: $10^{-3}$ with linear warmup over the first 10 epochs.
        *   Batch Size: 16.
        *   Epochs: 50.
        *   Loss Function: Binary Cross Entropy.
    *   **Zoo Model Training:**
        *   Encoder architecture: Two stacked two-head transformer blocks.
        *   Training duration: 100 epochs (checkpoints at 50, 75, 100, and best).

*   **Generalization on Low-Accuracy Models:** Visual analysis of scatterplots indicated that Transformer-NFN maintained strong predictive performance for low-accuracy networks, whereas baseline models showed greater variance and deviation from the ground truth in these regions.
*   **Dataset Distribution (MNIST):** The accuracy distribution for the MNIST-Transformers dataset was highly skewed, with a strong concentration of models in the 80% to 100% accuracy range and a near-uniform distribution across lower accuracies, with a slight increase around 10%.
*   **Dataset Distribution (AGNews):** The accuracy distribution for the AGNews-Transformers dataset showed a concentration in the 50% to 90% range, peaking around 80%, with a smaller distinct cluster of models around 25% accuracy.
*   **Robustness to Augmentation:** When the dataset was augmented using group action scaling transformations (ranges $[-1, 1]$, $[-10, 10]$, $[-100, 100]$), Transformer-NFN maintained or slightly improved its performance ($\approx 0.912-0.913$), whereas all baseline models suffered significant performance degradation (e.g., Random Forest dropped from 0.774 to $\approx 0.71$).
*   **Performance Gap:** The performance gap between Transformer-NFN and the next best baseline increased from 0.031 on the original dataset to approximately 0.08 on the augmented datasets.
*   **Component Importance:** Ablation studies indicated that the weights of the transformer block alone were sufficient to achieve a Kendall's $\tau$ score nearly identical to using all model components (0.909 vs 0.91 for AGNews). The classifier was the second most important component, followed by the embedding.
*   **Compactness:** Strong performance was achievable with relatively small Transformer-NFN configurations (e.g., dimension 15 with 1 layer achieved $\tau=0.913$), suggesting the model can be efficient.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex
\begin{figure}[h]
\begin{center}
%\framebox[4.0in]{$\;$}
\fbox{\rule[-.5cm]{0cm}{4cm} \rule[-.5cm]{4cm}{0cm}}
\end{center}
\caption{Sample figure caption.}
\end{figure}
```

### Example Code for Tables
```latex

\caption{Sample table title}
\label{sample-table}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---
### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.
- Attempt to recall or reconstruct any existing or published paper.
- Use external facts, assumptions, or prior familiarity with the work.
- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.
- Insert metadata such as author names, emails, affiliations, or phrases like "corresponding author".

#### Anonymity Requirement
The paper must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.  
Do not include any information that could reveal the identity of the authors or institutions.

#### Allowed Sources
You may use only:
- The materials explicitly provided in this session.
- Logical reasoning derived from those materials.

#### Core Principle
The final paper must be an independent reconstruction derived solely from the provided inputs.  
This constraint is strict and overrides all other instructions.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are typically treated as "black box" functions mapping inputs to outputs. However, a growing body of research in Neural Functional Networks (NFNs) treats the weights and gradients of DNNs as input data itself, enabling tasks such as weight editing, implicit representation processing, and learnable optimization. While NFNs have been rigorously developed for Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by leveraging permutation equivariance, there is currently no systematic framework for processing Transformer architectures.

Transformers possess a unique internal structure—specifically the Multi-Head Attention (MHA) mechanism—that exhibits complex symmetries beyond simple neuron permutation. The weights in a Transformer can be transformed (e.g., via specific invertible matrix multiplications and permutations of heads) without altering the function represented by the network. Current NFN architectures cannot account for these specific symmetries, rendering them inefficient or ineffective for processing Transformer weights. We need a rigorous mathematical characterization of the Transformer weight space and a novel NFN architecture designed to respect these symmetries.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose to develop **Transformer-NFN**, a specialized neural functional network that is equivariant to the maximal symmetric group of a standard Transformer block.

Our core hypothesis is that the functional equivalence of a Multi-Head Attention module is governed by the products of specific weight matrices (Query-Key and Value-Output), rather than the individual matrices in isolation. By formally deriving the group action $\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{U}}$ that leaves the Transformer function invariant, we can construct polynomial layers that share parameters according to the orbits of this group. We hypothesize that an architecture built on these principles will be able to process Transformer weights effectively by operating directly on the quotient space of the symmetries, thereby learning representations that are intrinsic to the function rather than the specific parameterization.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will execute this project in three phases: determining the symmetry group, defining the weight space and group action, and constructing the equivariant polynomial layers.

### 1. Characterization of Multi-Head Attention Symmetries

First, we will mathematically derive the necessary and sufficient conditions under which two sets of hyperparameters define the same Multi-Head Attention map.

Let the Multi-Head Attention map with $h$ heads be defined as:
$$
\mathrm{MultiHead}\left(X; W^{(O)}, \{W^{(Q,i)}, W^{(K,i)}, W^{(V,i)}\}_{i=1}^h\right) = \left( \bigoplus_{i=1}^h \mathrm{Head}\left(X; W^{(Q,i)}, W^{(K,i)}, W^{(V,i)}\right) \right) W^{(O)}
$$
We will treat the functional equivalence as dependent on the matrices $W^{(Q,i)}(W^{(K,i)})^\top$ and $W^{(V,i)}W^{(O,i)}$. We posit that the maximal symmetric group for the weights of the Multi-Head Attention is:
$$
\mathcal{G}_{\text{MHA}} = S_h \times \mathrm{GL}_{D_k}(\mathbb{R})^h \times \mathrm{GL}_{D_v}(\mathbb{R})^h
$$
where $S_h$ represents the permutation of heads, and the General Linear groups represent invertible transformations within the latent attention spaces.

### 2. Weight Space and Group Action Definition

We will define the weight space $\mathcal{U}$ of a standard transformer block, denoted as $\mathrm{Attn}$. The block transforms input $\boldsymbol{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times D}$ via:
$$
\mathrm{Attn}(X) = \mathrm{LayerNorm}\left(\mathrm{ReLU}\left(\hat{X} \cdot W^{(A)} + \mathbf{1}_L \cdot b^{(A)}\right) \cdot W^{(B)} + \mathbf{1}_L \cdot b^{(B)}\right)
$$
where $\hat{X}$ is the normalized output of the Multi-Head Attention. The weight space $\mathcal{U}$ consists of tuples:
$$
U = \left( \left( W^{(Q,i)}, W^{(K,i)}, W^{(V,i)}, W^{(O,i)} \right)_{i=1,\dots,h}, (W^{(A)}, W^{(B)}), (b^{(A)}, b^{(B)}) \right)
$$
We will define the full symmetry group $\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{U}}$ acting on this space as:
$$
\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{U}} = S_h \times \mathrm{GL}_{D_k}(\mathbb{R})^h \times \mathrm{GL}_{D_v}(\mathbb{R})^h \times \mathcal{P}_D \times \mathcal{P}_{D_A}
$$
Here, $\mathcal{P}_D$ and $\mathcal{P}_{D_A}$ represent permutation matrices corresponding to neuron rearrangements in the hidden layers. An element $g \in \mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{U}}$ acts on $U$ via the following transformation rules, which we will enforce in our network design:
$$
\begin{aligned}
[gW]^{(Q,i)} &= W^{(Q,\tau(i))} \cdot (M^{(\tau(i))})^\top \\
[gW]^{(K,i)} &= W^{(K,\tau(i))} \cdot (M^{(\tau(i))})^{-1} \\
[gW]^{(V,i)} &= W^{(V,\tau(i))} \cdot N^{(\tau(i))} \\
[gW]^{(O,i)} &= (N^{(\tau(i))})^{-1} \cdot W^{(O,\tau(i))} \cdot P_{\pi_O} \\
[gW]^{(A)} &= P_{\pi_O}^{-1} \cdot W^{(A)} \cdot P_{\pi_A} \\
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\tau \in S_h$, matrices $M, N$ are invertible scaling/rotation matrices, and $P$ are permutation matrices.

### 3. Construction of Transformer-NFN Architecture

We will construct the Transformer-NFN using **Equivariant Polynomial Layers**. The main building block will be a map $\mathcal{E}: \mathcal{U} \to \mathcal{U}$ that commutes with the group action, i.e., $\mathcal{E}(gU) = g\mathcal{E}(U)$.

To maintain expressivity while respecting the product-based symmetries of attention, we will augment the input space with quadratic terms. We define:
$$
[WW]^{(QK, i)} := W^{(Q,i)} \cdot (W^{(K,i)})^\top, \quad \text{and} \quad [WW]^{(VO, i)} := W^{(V,i)} \cdot W^{(O,i)}
$$
The layer output for a weight component (e.g., $W^{(Q,i)}$) will be formulated as a linear combination of the input weights and these quadratic terms, utilizing a parameter-sharing scheme $\Phi$ derived from the group constraints.

For example, the invariant polynomial layer $I(U)$ (readout layer) will be constructed as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
I(U) &= \sum_{p=1}^D \sum_{q=1}^D \Phi_{(QK,\bullet) \cdot p, q} \cdot \left( \sum_{s=1}^h [WW]_{p,q}^{(QK, s)} \right) \\
&+ \sum_{p=1}^D \sum_{q=1}^D \Phi_{(VO,\bullet) \cdot p, \bullet} \cdot \left( \sum_{s=1}^h [WW]_{p,q}^{(VO, s)} \right) \\
&+ \sum_{p=1}^D \sum_{q=1}^{D_A} \Phi_{(A) \cdot \bullet, \bullet} \cdot [W]_{p,q}^{(A)} + \dots
\end{aligned}
$$
In this formulation, the notation $\bullet$ indicates indices over which the coefficients $\Phi$ must remain constant (parameter sharing) to ensure invariance under permutations and independence from the specific head index $s$.

We will implement these layers using tensor contraction operations (e.g., `einsum`) that rigorously enforce the parameter sharing constraints required by $\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{U}}$. The architecture will consist of stacked equivariant layers followed by a final invariant layer to produce the target output.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Theoretical Foundation:** We will establish the first rigorous characterization of the maximal symmetric group of Transformer weights, proving the necessary and sufficient conditions for functional equivalence in Multi-Head Attention.
2.  **Novel Architecture:** We will introduce the **Transformer-NFN**, the first neural functional network architecture specifically designed to be equivariant to the complex continuous and discrete symmetries of Transformers (scaling, rotation, and permutation).
3.  **Design Principles:** We will provide a systematic methodology for constructing polynomial layers that operate on weight spaces involving product-based symmetries, extending the scope of Deep Learning on Deep Learning beyond simple MLPs and CNNs.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
